documents.title: Vaccines for preventing infections in adults with solid tumours.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Infections are one of the most frequent complications seen in adults with cancer, often arising from the underlying condition or as a result of immunosuppressive treatments. Certain infections (e.g. influenza, pneumococcal disease, and meningococcal disease) may be prevented through vaccination. However, adults with solid tumours may elicit varying immune responses compared to healthy individuals.
OBJECTIVES: To assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of infectious diseases in adults with solid tumours.
SEARCH METHODS: We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, two further databases, and two study registries from inception to 2 December 2024 for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and controlled non-randomised studies of interventions (NRSIs).
SELECTION CRITERIA: We included RCTs evaluating vaccines against the following infectious diseases in adults (≥ 18 years of age) with any diagnosis of solid tumour cancer compared to placebo or no vaccine: pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, diphtheria, influenza, herpes zoster, and COVID-19. In cases where RCTs were unavailable, we included prospective controlled NRSIs. We excluded live-attenuated vaccines.
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: We followed standard Cochrane methodology. Two review authors independently screened search results, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias (RoB) in the included studies using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool for RCTs and ROBINS-I for NRSIs. We rated the certainty in the evidence using the GRADE approach for the following prioritised outcomes: incidence of infection concerned, all-cause mortality, quality of life, adverse events (AEs) of any grade, serious adverse events (SAEs), localised events at the injection site, and systemic events.
MAIN RESULTS: We included 10 studies (five RCTs and five NRSIs) involving 81,823 adults with solid tumours receiving vaccines to prevent infections with herpes zoster, influenza, or COVID-19. Six studies included participants with varied solid tumours, while two focused on neck and oesophageal cancer or lung cancer. We assessed the RCTs to be at low or moderate risk of bias, whereas most NRSIs were at critical risk of bias due to concerns about confounding. We identified two ongoing studies: one RCT evaluating an influenza vaccine, and one NRSI evaluating COVID-19 vaccines. Twelve studies are awaiting assessment. We did not identify RCTs or NRSIs of vaccines for preventing pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, or diphtheria compared to placebo or no vaccine. The results from the RCTs are presented below. The results from the NRSIs are detailed in the main text of the review. No study reported quality of life. Vaccines for preventing herpes zoster compared to placebo or no vaccine Three RCTs (3054 participants) evaluated vaccines to prevent herpes zoster. Herpes zoster vaccines decrease the incidence of herpes zoster up to 29.4 months after the final dose (RR 0.37, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.59; 1 RCT, 2678 participants; high-certainty evidence). Herpes zoster vaccines probably make little or no difference to all-cause mortality up to 28 days after the final dose (RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.50; 2 RCTs, 2744 participants; moderate-certainty evidence); make little or no difference to any-grade AEs up to 30 days after final dose (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.05; 3 RCTs, 2976 participants; high-certainty evidence), and probably make little or no difference in SAEs up to 30 days (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.24; I² = 0%; 3 RCTs, 2976 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster increase the number of participants with localised events at the injection site compared to placebo or no vaccine (RR 6.81, 95% CI 2.52 to 18.40; 3 RCTs, 2966 participants; high-certainty evidence) and may make little or no difference to the number of participants with systemic events up to 30 days after final dose (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.50; 3 RCTs, 2966 participants; low-certainty evidence). Vaccines for preventing influenza compared to placebo or no vaccine One RCT (75 participants) evaluated vaccines to prevent influenza. We are uncertain about the effects of influenza vaccines administered prior to surgery on all-cause mortality (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.07 to 15.33; 1 RCT, 66 participants; very low-certainty evidence), any-grade AEs (RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.54; 1 RCT, 75 participants; very low-certainty evidence), and SAEs (RR 1.46, 95% CI 0.76 to 2.83; 1 RCT, 75 participants; very low-certainty evidence) up to 15 days post-surgery. The RCT did not report the incidence of influenza, localised events at the injection site, or systemic events. Vaccines for preventing COVID-19 compared to placebo or no vaccine One RCT (2256 participants) evaluated vaccines to prevent COVID-19. Participants may have been exposed to the SARS-CoV-2 variants alpha, beta, and gamma. Vaccines to prevent COVID-19 probably decrease the incidence of COVID-19 in participants without previous COVID-19 infection up to six months after the second dose (RR 0.08, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.25; 1 RCT, 2100 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). The COVID-19 vaccines probably increase any-grade AEs (RR 1.99, 95% CI 1.71 to 2.30; 1 RCT, 2328 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). They may have little or no effect on SAEs up to 6 months after the second dose (RR 1.43, 95% CI 0.80 to 2.54; 1 RCT, 2328 participants; low-certainty evidence). The RCT did not report localised events at the injection site or systemic events.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: In adults with solid tumours, herpes zoster vaccines reduced the incidence of herpes zoster (high-certainty evidence), although localised events at the injection site were more likely to occur (high-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain about the effects of influenza vaccines on all-cause mortality, any-grade AEs, and SAEs (very low-certainty evidence); the incidence of influenza was not measured in the studies. COVID-19 vaccines probably decrease the incidence of COVID-19 in those without prior infection (moderate-certainty evidence) but probably increase any-grade AEs (moderate-certainty evidence). We found no RCTs or NRSIs investigating vaccines for preventing pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, diphtheria compared to placebo or no vaccine, in adults with solid tumours. Additional research, preferably of RCT design, is necessary to resolve uncertainties.

Vaccines for the prevention of infections in adults with solid tumors 2023 5 10 5 2023 CD015551 The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 10.1002/14651858.CD015551 PMC10171243 Abstract Background Infections are one of the most frequent complications seen in adults with cancer, often arising from the underlying condition or as a result of immunosuppressive treatments. Certain infections (e.g. influenza, pneumococcal disease, and meningococcal disease) may be prevented through vaccination. However, adults with solid tumours may elicit varying immune responses compared to healthy individuals. Objectives To assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of infectious diseases in adults with solid tumours. Search methods We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, two further databases, and two study registries from inception to 2 December 2024 for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and controlled non‐randomised studies of interventions (NRSIs). Selection criteria We included RCTs evaluating vaccines against the following infectious diseases in adults (≥ 18 years of age) with any diagnosis of solid tumour cancer compared to placebo or no vaccine: pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, diphtheria, influenza, herpes zoster, and COVID‐19. In cases where RCTs were unavailable, we included prospective controlled NRSIs. We excluded live‐attenuated vaccines. Data collection and analysis We followed standard Cochrane methodology. Two review authors independently screened search results, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias (RoB) in the included studies using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool for RCTs and ROBINS‐I for NRSIs. We rated the certainty in the evidence using the GRADE approach for the following prioritised outcomes: incidence of infection concerned, all‐cause mortality, quality of life, adverse events (AEs) of any grade, serious adverse events (SAEs), localised events at the injection site, and systemic events. Main results We included 10 studies (five RCTs and five NRSIs) involving 81,823 adults with solid tumours receiving vaccines to prevent infections with herpes zoster, influenza, or COVID‐19. Six studies included participants with varied solid tumours, while two focused on neck and oesophageal cancer or lung cancer. We assessed the RCTs to be at low or moderate risk of bias, whereas most NRSIs were at critical risk of bias due to concerns about confounding. We identified two ongoing studies: one RCT evaluating an influenza vaccine, and one NRSI evaluating COVID‐19 vaccines. Twelve studies are awaiting assessment. We did not identify RCTs or NRSIs of vaccines for preventing pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, or diphtheria compared to placebo or no vaccine. The results from the RCTs are presented below. The results from the NRSIs are detailed in the main text of the review. No study reported quality of life. Vaccines for preventing herpes zoster compared to placebo or no vaccine Three RCTs (3054 participants) evaluated vaccines to prevent herpes zoster. Herpes zoster vaccines decrease the incidence of herpes zoster up to 29.4 months after the final dose (RR 0.37, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.59; 1 RCT, 2678 participants; high‐certainty evidence). Herpes zoster vaccines probably make little or no difference to all‐cause mortality up to 28 days after the final dose (RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.50; 2 RCTs, 2744 participants; moderate‐certainty evidence); make little or no difference to any‐grade AEs up to 30 days after final dose (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.05; 3 RCTs, 2976 participants; high‐certainty evidence), and probably make little or no difference in SAEs up to 30 days (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.24; I² = 0%; 3 RCTs, 2976 participants; moderate‐certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster increase the number of participants with localised events at the injection site compared to placebo or no vaccine (RR 6.81, 95% CI 2.52 to 18.40; 3 RCTs, 2966 participants; high‐certainty evidence) and may make little or no difference to the number of participants with systemic events up to 30 days after final dose (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.50; 3 RCTs, 2966 participants; low‐certainty evidence). Vaccines for preventing influenza compared to placebo or no vaccine One RCT (75 participants) evaluated vaccines to prevent influenza. We are uncertain about the effects of influenza vaccines administered prior to surgery on all‐cause mortality (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.07 to 15.33; 1 RCT, 66 participants; very low‐certainty evidence), any‐grade AEs (RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.54; 1 RCT, 75 participants; very low‐certainty evidence), and SAEs (RR 1.46, 95% CI 0.76 to 2.83; 1 RCT, 75 participants; very low‐certainty evidence) up to 15 days post‐surgery. The RCT did not report the incidence of influenza, localised events at the injection site, or systemic events. Vaccines for preventing COVID‐19 compared to placebo or no vaccine One RCT (2256 participants) evaluated vaccines to prevent COVID‐19. Participants may have been exposed to the SARS‐CoV‐2 variants alpha, beta, and gamma. Vaccines to prevent COVID‐19 probably decrease the incidence of COVID‐19 in participants without previous COVID‐19 infection up to six months after the second dose (RR 0.08, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.25; 1 RCT, 2100 participants; moderate‐certainty evidence). The COVID‐19 vaccines probably increase any‐grade AEs (RR 1.99, 95% CI 1.71 to 2.30; 1 RCT, 2328 participants; moderate‐certainty evidence). They may have little or no effect on SAEs up to 6 months after the second dose (RR 1.43, 95% CI 0.80 to 2.54; 1 RCT, 2328 participants; low‐certainty evidence). The RCT did not report localised events at the injection site or systemic events. Authors' conclusions In adults with solid tumours, herpes zoster vaccines reduced the incidence of herpes zoster (high‐certainty evidence), although localised events at the injection site were more likely to occur (high‐certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain about the effects of influenza vaccines on all‐cause mortality, any‐grade AEs, and SAEs (very low‐certainty evidence); the incidence of influenza was not measured in the studies. COVID‐19 vaccines probably decrease the incidence of COVID‐19 in those without prior infection (moderate‐certainty evidence) but probably increase any‐grade AEs (moderate‐certainty evidence). We found no RCTs or NRSIs investigating vaccines for preventing pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, diphtheria compared to placebo or no vaccine, in adults with solid tumours. Additional research, preferably of RCT design, is necessary to resolve uncertainties. Plain language summary What are the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of infectious diseases in adults with cancer (solid tumours)? Key messages ‐ In adults with cancer (solid tumours), vaccines to prevent herpes zoster reduce the occurrence of herpes zoster but increase unwanted effects such as pain or redness at the injection site. ‐ We are uncertain about the effects of influenza vaccines on death from any cause, unwanted effects of any severity, and serious unwanted effects. The occurrence of influenza was not measured. ‐ Vaccines to prevent COVID‐19 probably reduce the occurrence of COVID‐19 but probably increase unwanted effects of any severity. ‐ Further research is needed. Why prevent infections in adults with cancer? Adults with cancer often experience infections as a complication, either due to their underlying condition or treatments that lead to immunosuppression. Some infections can be prevented through vaccination. How do vaccines work? The primary aim of vaccination is to prevent infection. Due to altered immune function, adults with solid tumours may have different immune responses to vaccination than those of the healthy population. However, immunosuppression (reduced effectiveness of the immune system) may vary amongst people with solid tumours depending on the underlying disease and type of treatment. What did we want to find out? We wanted to find out how well vaccines work in preventing infectious diseases in adults (≥ 18 years of age) with solid tumours (not blood cancer). We looked at: ‐ the occurrence of infections against which vaccination was given; ‐ death from any cause; ‐ quality of life; ‐ unwanted effects (any severity); ‐ serious unwanted effects, such as life‐threatening conditions, hospitalisation, disability, or death; ‐ reactions at the injection site, such as pain or redness; and ‐ systemic (i.e. affecting the whole body) reactions like fever, headache, or fatigue. What did we do? We searched for studies comparing vaccines against various infectious diseases (e.g. pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, diphtheria, influenza, herpes zoster, and COVID‐19) versus placebo (fake treatment) or no vaccination in adults with solid tumours. We included randomised and non‐randomised studies. We summarised the results from the studies and rated our confidence in the research evidence. What did we find? We found 10 studies (five randomised and five non‐randomised studies) that involved 81,823 adults with cancer and assessed vaccines to prevent infection with herpes zoster, influenza or COVID‐19. We did not identify studies of vaccines to prevent pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, diphtheria compared to placebo or no vaccine. We present the results from randomised studies below. Results from non‐randomised studies are in the full review. Main results Vaccines for preventing herpes zoster compared to placebo or no vaccine in adults with solid tumours: ‐ reduce the occurrence of herpes zoster up to 29.4 months after the final dose (1 study, 2678 adults); ‐ may make little or no difference in death from any cause up to 28 days after the final dose (2 studies, 2744 adults); ‐ make little or no difference in unwanted effects of any severity and serious unwanted effects up to 30 days after the final dose (3 studies, 2976 adults); ‐ increase pain or redness at the injection site and may make little or no difference in systemic reactions up to 30 days after the final dose (3 studies, 2966 adults). We found no information about quality of life. Vaccines for preventing influenza compared to placebo or no vaccine in adults with solid tumours ‐ We are uncertain about the impact of influenza vaccines given before surgery on death from any cause up to 15 days after surgery (1 study, 66 adults). ‐ We are uncertain about the impact of influenza vaccines given before surgery on unwanted effects (any severity) and serious unwanted effects up to 15 days after surgery (1 study, 75 adults). We found no information about the incidence of influenza, quality of life, pain or redness at the injection site, or systemic reactions. Vaccines for preventing COVID‐19 compared to placebo or no vaccine in adults with solid tumours ‐ probably reduce the occurrence of COVID‐19 in adults without previous COVID‐19 infection up to six months after the second dose (1 study, 2100 adults); ‐ probably increase unwanted effects of any severity (1 study, 2328 adults); ‐ may make little or no difference in serious unwanted effects (1 study, 2328 adults). We found no data on all‐cause mortality, quality of life, pain or redness at the injection site, or systemic reactions. What are the limitations of the evidence? We did not identify studies for all infectious diseases. Our confidence in the evidence we found ranged from high to very low, primarily due to problems within the studies, such as the potential for risk of bias and imprecise results. Most non‐randomised studies were too problematic to provide reliable evidence. The studies did not report everything that we were interested in, including quality of life. How up to date is this evidence? Background Description of the condition Cancer is a leading cause of death in most countries ( Sung 2021 ). In 2020, cancer caused almost 10 million deaths globally ( WHO 2022 ). In the USA, there will be an estimated 2,041,910 new cancer cases and 618,120 cancer deaths in the year 2025. Breast, prostate, lung, and colon cancers are the most common types of cancer ( Siegel 2025 ). Infections are one of the most frequent complications seen in people with cancer. They occur as a result of the underlying condition or as a consequence of immunosuppressive therapies. People with haematological malignancies usually have higher levels of immunosuppression than those with solid tumours, because neoplastic processes affect the host immune system, and treatments usually cause prolonged neutropenia ( Rolston 2017 ). Thus, the incidence of infections is lower in people with solid tumours compared to those with haematological malignancies ( Marin 2014 ; Schelenz 2013 ). Nevertheless, next to person‐related factors, such as age, sex, comorbidity, and malnutrition, other common risk factors for infection in people with solid tumours include tumour obstruction (e.g. in people with lung, hepatobiliary, pancreatic, and intestinal cancers), oncological surgery, disruption of anatomic barriers (e.g. skin and mucosal surfaces), and invasive procedures. Common infection sites are the respiratory and urinary tract, bloodstream, and skin ( Rolston 2017 ). Bacterial infections are the most common type of infection in people with cancer, followed by viral and fungal infections ( Cancer 2024 ). People with cancer are at an increased risk of developing severe disease that can lead to worse outcomes than those of the healthy population ( Hosseini‐Moghaddam 2023 ). Anti‐infective therapies, such as antibiotics, antifungals, and antivirals, can interfere with anticancer agents, potentially leading to reduced efficacy and increased toxicity ( Zhang 2021 ). This often necessitates the postponement of anticancer therapies to address infections or delays in administering anti‐infective therapies until after the completion of cancer treatment ( Zorina 2015 ). Some infections (e.g. influenza, pneumococcal disease, and meningococcal disease) can be prevented through vaccination ( ECDC 2025 ). Therefore, implementing preventive strategies such as vaccinations may help people undergoing cancer treatment to avoid infection. Description of the intervention Vaccines can be broadly classified according to the types of pathogens used in their development. Conventional vaccines include live‐attenuated pathogens (e.g. measles, rubella, mumps), inactivated pathogens (e.g. polio, first influenza vaccines), and conjugate vaccines (e.g. influenza, human papillomavirus, hepatitis B). In contrast, novel vaccine technologies leverage genome‐sequence information and include nucleic acid vaccines and vector‐based vaccines ( Gebre 2021 ; Rüthrich 2022 ). Live‐attenuated vaccines contain weakened or attenuated pathogens, mimicking a natural infection. In healthy individuals, these vaccines trigger a strong cellular and humoral immune response without causing the disease itself ( Rüthrich 2022 ). In people who are immunocompromised, these vaccines are contraindicated because of the risk of severe disease ( Kamboj 2024 ; Kamei 2023 ). Inactivated vaccines are created by culturing pathogens and then killing them using methods such as heat or formaldehyde. Although these vaccines lose their virulence, they still provoke an immune response by generating specific antibodies against parts of the pathogen. However, inactivated vaccines typically result in weaker immune responses compared to live‐attenuated vaccines. This often means that multiple doses are needed to achieve effective protection. They are particularly suitable for individuals with weakened immune systems ( Jain 2021 ). Conjugate vaccines combine weak antigens (often polysaccharides from bacterial capsules) with strong antigens (usually proteins) to enhance the immune response. This combination helps activate T cells, which subsequently stimulate B cells to produce antibodies against the weak antigen. By inducing T cell activation, conjugate vaccines provide effective protection against certain infections but may still require booster doses ( Jain 2021 ). Nucleic acid vaccines use genetic material from a pathogen, either deoxyribonucleic (DNA) or ribonucleic acid (RNA), to stimulate an immune response. This genetic material provides instructions for producing specific proteins that the immune system recognises as foreign antigens. Once inside host cells, this genetic information is used to produce antigens that activate the immune response ( Sagili Anthony 2021 ). Vector‐based vaccines use modified viruses as delivery vehicles to introduce genes into host cells. These viral vectors have been altered to remove harmful genes while keeping their ability to enter cells effectively. For example, the ChAdOx1 nCoV‐19 vaccine uses a modified chimpanzee adenovirus to deliver the gene for the SARS‐CoV‐2 spike protein into the cells. Inside the cell, this gene is turned into messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA), which directs the production of antigens that trigger an immune response. While not all nucleic acid or vector‐based vaccines will necessarily require boosters, many do, particularly in light of evolving pathogens and varying immune responses amongst different populations ( Deng 2022 ; Jain 2021 ). How the intervention might work The primary purpose of vaccination is to prevent infection. It may also decrease the severity of infections, avoid hospitalisations, and reduce infection‐related mortality ( Mikulska 2019 ). Common side effects of vaccination include fever, myalgia, and headaches. These symptoms are non‐specific and can arise from various causes beyond vaccination. Additionally, localised reactions at the injection site, including pain, swelling, and redness, may occur in a range of individuals, with reported frequencies varying between 5% to 60% across different vaccine types ( Gecgel 2024 ). Generally mild and temporary, these side effects typically resolve within 24 to 48 hours post‐vaccination. The incidence and nature of these side effects are comparable to those observed in the general population ( Gecgel 2024 ; Shear 2023 ). The immune response to vaccination varies amongst individuals, influenced by a wide array of factors. Recognising these factors is essential for enhancing vaccine efficacy and immunogenicity. According to Zimmermann 2019 , one category of factors is intrinsic host characteristics, including age, sex, and comorbidities. For instance, immune function tends to decline with age, leading to differences in how younger and older individuals respond to vaccines. Additionally, sex‐related biological differences can result in varying immune responses. Research indicates that females often exhibit higher antibody responses to certain vaccines than males ( Zimmermann 2019 ). Pre‐existing health conditions also play a critical role in vaccine responses. Adults with haematological disorders typically elicit lower immune responses to most vaccines when compared to healthy individuals. Individuals with solid tumours may show either adequate or lower immune responses when compared to healthy individuals, with variations depending on the type of malignancy and its stage ( Becerril‐Gaitan 2022 ; Nordøy 2002 ; Vollaard 2017 ). Berber 2024 highlights the impact of different therapeutic approaches and the timing of vaccination in relation to treatment status on vaccine efficacy. Vaccine‐related factors are also important; for example, mRNA COVID‐19 vaccines have shown the highest effectiveness amongst COVID‐19 vaccines ( Berber 2024 ). Furthermore, administration factors such as the interval between vaccinations and whether a heterologous or homologous approach is used are important considerations. Heterologous schedules involve administering different vaccines for different doses, while homologous schedules utilise the same vaccine throughout, and both strategies can lead to distinct immunological outcomes ( Berber 2024 ). According to the European Conference on Infections in Leukaemia guidelines for people with cancer after stem cell transplantation, limited evidence indicates that re‐vaccination after stem cell transplantation should be considered ( Cordonnier 2019 ). For adults with haematological malignancies who are not candidates for stem cell transplantation, vaccination against influenza and pneumococcal disease is recommended. No clear recommendations are given for other vaccinations for this population due to lack of evidence ( Mikulska 2019 ). The Infectious Diseases Working Party of the German Society for Hematology and Medical Oncology provides recommendations based on expert panel discussion but lacks transparency regarding literature selection, bias assessment, or analysis of identified studies ( Rieger 2018 ). The American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) provides recommendations for adults with haematological malignancies and solid tumours ( Kamboj 2024 ). The influenza vaccine is recommended annually for all ages. The COVID‐19 vaccine is recommended to be administered according to the latest schedule from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) ( CDC 2024 ). The recombinant zoster vaccine is recommended for adults aged 19 years and older, with two doses given at least four weeks apart. Additionally, individuals aged 19 years and older should receive one dose of the 15‐valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV15), followed by the 23‐valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) eight weeks later or alternatively, a single dose of PCV20. Vaccination is ideally recommended two to four weeks prior to the initiation of cancer treatment. Non‐live vaccines may also be administered during or after chemotherapy, immunotherapy, hormonal treatment, radiation, or surgery. These recommendations are grounded in evidence‐based research ( Kamboj 2024 ). The Canadian Immunization Guide for people with haematological disorders and solid tumours aligns with ASCO's recommendations ( Government of Canada 2024 ; Kamboj 2024 ). It highlights the importance of timely vaccination prior to cancer treatment while considering individual health circumstances as well as the need for healthcare professionals to actively promote vaccination as a part of comprehensive cancer care ( Government of Canada 2024 ). The Italian Association of Medical Oncology (AIOM) focuses specifically on adults with solid tumours and offers detailed guidance regarding influenza, pneumococcal, and COVID‐19 vaccinations. The AIOM emphasises optimal timing relative to treatment phases, booster schedules, vaccinating close contacts, and healthcare worker involvement. It recommends pneumococcal vaccination for all cancer patients aged 65 years and older, as well as younger patients with lung or head and neck cancers. While the optimal frequency for the COVID‐19 vaccine booster is unclear, the AIOM suggests not exceeding a 12‐month interval between booster doses ( Pedrazzoli 2023 ). For adults with haematological disorders, a single dose of the Haemophilus influenzae type b (HiB) vaccine is recommended, regardless of prior vaccinations. Those with severe neutropenia (neutrophil counts under 500/µL) should avoid vaccination due to the risk of acute febrile episodes ( Australian Government 2020 ). Live‐attenuated vaccines are contraindicated in adults with cancer ( Government of Canada 2024 ; Kamboj 2024 ; Pedrazzoli 2023 ). Why it is important to do this review The research question of how to prevent vaccine‐preventable infections in people with cancer has been prioritised by the German Society for Hematology and Medical Oncology (DGHO). In 2019, the DGHO created a roadmap for research on cancer and diseases of the blood, summarising the current essential research questions ( DGHO 2019 ). Prevention of infections in people with cancer was one of the essential research fields identified in this process. According to the DGHO, vaccines offer the best option because of tolerability and costs for prevention in the field of pharmacological prophylaxis. They also note that there is insufficient evidence to support the belief that individuals with cancer have a weaker response to vaccines compared to the general population. When cancer patients begin their antineoplastic therapies for cancer treatment, there is currently no recommendation suggesting that researchers should investigate how these treatments might affect the effectiveness of vaccinations. This indicates a gap in research regarding how cancer therapies could influence vaccine responses. The ASCO guidelines also highlight critical gaps in the vaccination of cancer patients that require ongoing research. They emphasise the importance of including diverse patient populations with various types of immunocompromise in vaccine trials, ensuring that actively or recently treated patients are represented. Additionally, there is a pressing need to develop more immunogenic vaccines and optimise vaccination strategies for those receiving novel therapies, particularly as these populations may have unique immune challenges due to their underlying conditions and previous treatments ( Kamboj 2024 ). Although there is a Cochrane review, last updated in 2018 ( Bitterman 2018 ), that primarily focuses on influenza vaccines for all types of cancer (solid and haematological malignancies, and post‐autologous or allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation), this review included various study designs, including randomized controlled trials (RCT), prospective cohort studies, and retrospective studies, such as case‐control studies. However, retrospective studies are often at high risk of bias. Therefore, the exclusion of evidence from retrospective study designs enhances reliability. Our review focuses on individuals with solid tumours. It is part of a series of reviews focusing on people with haematological malignancies ( Zorger 2025 (not yet published) ) and cellular therapies (including autologous and allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation and chimeric antigen receptor T‐cell) (proposed title: Vaccines for the prevention of infections in adult patients with cellular therapies ). Objectives To assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of infectious diseases in adults with solid tumours. Methods Criteria for considering studies for this review Types of studies We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs). For RCT data, we used the common methods recommended by the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions ( Higgins 2024a ). We had planned to include non‐standard RCT designs, such as cluster‐randomised studies (using methods as recommended in Chapter 23 of the Cochrane Handbook ( Higgins 2024b )) and cross‐over studies, but have not identified any. In cross‐over studies, we would only consider results from the first period before cross‐over to avoid carry‐over effects. If we did not find at least one RCT per vaccine for each infectious disease, we included prospectively registered, controlled non‐randomised studies of interventions (NRSIs) for this disease, including quasi‐RCTs, using methods proposed in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions ( Reeves 2024 ). As a post hoc change, we searched for controlled NRSIs for vaccines against influenza and COVID‐19, even though we identified at least one RCT for each, as the RCT on influenza vaccines was published only as correspondence, while the RCT on COVID‐19 included participants with solid tumours in a post hoc subgroup analysis. We only considered studies with a minimum sample size of 20 participants per arm to ensure adequate statistical power and reliability of the results, allowing for more robust conclusions and reducing the risk of type I and type II errors ( Ioannidis 2005 ; Nüesch 2010 ). We excluded non‐comparative study designs (e.g. case series) and retrospective studies, because they are often of low methodological quality and more prone to bias (e.g. through selective inclusion of participants or missing entries in patient files ( Norris 2005 )). We decided to include formats such as full‐text publications, preprints, abstract publications, results published in study registries, and information provided by the principal investigators. There was no limit with respect to the length of follow‐up. Types of participants We considered studies examining adult participants (i.e. at least 18 years of age) with any diagnosis of a solid tumour (e.g. breast, colon, bladder, prostate, or lung), diagnosed with any stage (0, I, II, III, or IV ( Brierley 2016 )), including people with relapsed or metastatic disease. Studies including people with cancer and other entities were only included if the study authors provided subgroup data for participants with solid tumours. We included studies of people receiving antineoplastic treatment or no treatment, but excluded data from individuals receiving cellular therapies (e.g. autologous and allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation and chimeric antigen receptor T‐cell), as they will be addressed in another review. Types of interventions We included vaccines for the prevention of the following infectious diseases in adults with solid tumours. Inactivated and conjugate vaccines Pneumococcal disease Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) disease Meningococcal disease Pertussis Hepatitis B Tetanus Polio Diphtheria Influenza Herpes zoster Novel vaccine technologies COVID‐19. We included COVID‐19 vaccines authorised by the European Medicines Agencies (EMA) or authorised in at least 10 countries worldwide by the time of the search (according to McGill COVID‐19 Vaccine Tracker Team ( McGill 2021 ), available from covid19.trackvaccines.org/). As of 30 August 2023, those were: BNT162b2; BNT162b2 Bivalent WT/OMI BA.1; BNT162b2 Bivalent WT/OMI BA.4/BA.5 (Comirnaty; Biontech Pfizer); mRNA1273; mRNA‐1273.214 Original/Omicron BA.1; mRNA‐1273.222 Original/Omicron BA.4/BA.5 (Spikevax; Moderna); AZD12222 (Vaxzevria; AstraZeneca); Ad26.COV2.S (COVID‐19 Vaccine Janssen); Sputnik V (Gamaleya); Sputnik Light (Gamaleya); BBIBP‐CorV* (Sinopharm; Beijing CNBG); CoronaVac* (Sinovac); BBV152* (Covaxin); Ad5‐nCoV (Convidecia); NVX‐CoV2373 (Nuvaxovid; Novavax); VidPrevtyn Beta (Sanofi/GSK); VLA2001* (Valneva). *These COVID‐19 vaccines are inactivated vaccines. A combination of vaccines that includes at least one eligible vaccine We excluded live‐attenuated vaccines because these are contraindicated in people with immunocompromised systems. As a comparator, we accepted placebo or no vaccine. Types of outcome measures The outcomes of interest were prioritised by clinical experts, people with cancer, and their representatives. Critical outcome Incidence of the infection concerned (method of measurement as defined in the study) Important outcomes All‐cause mortality (at longest follow‐up available) Quality of life (QoL), if measured using reliable and valid instruments, such as the European Organisation for the Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Questionnaire (EORT‐QLQ C30; Fayers 2002 ), Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy‐General ( FACT‐G; Cella 1993 ) or Quality of Life Scale ( QOLS; Burckhardt 2003 ); at a time point most commonly reported in the studies; if the reported time points differ significantly, we had planned to choose the longest follow‐up available, but there were no data available. Number of participants with adverse events (AEs) of any grade at longest follow‐up available Number of participants with serious adverse events (SAEs) at longest follow‐up available Number of participants with localised effects at the injection site (e.g. tenderness or soreness, erythema, arm stiffness), at the longest follow‐up available Number of participants with systemic events (e.g. myalgia, fever, headache, fatigue, rash) at the longest follow‐up available Hierarchy of outcome measures If the same outcome domain was measured in multiple ways within one study or across multiple studies (e.g. QoL measured on two different scales), we had planned to prioritise the outcome measure most commonly reported in studies. However, this scenario did not arise. Timing of outcome measures We considered outcome data for all published time points after full vaccination (i.e. for most vaccines, two weeks after the last planned injection). When sufficient data were available, we grouped the measurement time points of eligible outcomes into short‐term (up to 12 weeks after full vaccination), medium‐term (from 12 weeks to 6 months after full vaccination) and long‐term (more than 6 months after full vaccination) observations. Eligible studies that did not report any of the aforementioned outcomes were categorised as 'awaiting classification'. Consumer involvement During the protocol development, we invited people with cancer and their representatives from two German cancer self‐help groups to be involved and share their opinions and perspectives regarding the most patient‐relevant research objectives, interventions, and outcomes to be addressed by this systematic review. Nine participants took part in an interactive online workshop. Through discussion, we identified that participants were most interested in COVID‐19 vaccines, seasonal vaccines (such as influenza), and vaccinations that need to be refreshed, such as diphtheria and tetanus. The most patient‐relevant outcomes were efficacy, interactions with cancer drugs, and adverse events. However, the number of vaccines required and the duration of immunity after vaccination were considered less important by the participants. The findings of the workshop were directly considered in the development of the protocol. In a second workshop, we presented preliminary findings of the review. Search methods for identification of studies Electronic searches Our information specialist (IM) adapted the search strategies for electronic databases based on the suggestions in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions ( Lefebvre 2022 ). In this emerging field, we expected that at least the abstract would be published in English. If the full‐text articles were published in other languages, we had planned to use Cochrane Engage to identify people within Cochrane to translate these studies ( https://engage.cochrane.org/ ), but no translation was needed. Our search was run to identify studies for the following two reviews. Vaccines for the prevention of infections in adults with solid tumours Vaccines for the prevention of infections in adults with haematological malignancies (from the Cochrane review by Zorger 2025 (not yet published) ) We searched the following databases from 1 January 1946 to 2 December 2024 for RCTs ( Appendix 1 ) and for controlled NRSIs ( Appendix 2 ), if not at least one RCT per infectious disease was available. Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) in the Cochrane Library (issue 12, 2024) MEDLINE Ovid (1946 to 2 December 2024) Embase Ovid (1974 to 2 December 2024) Web of Science Emerging Sources Citation Index (ESCI; 2017 to 2 December 2024) LILACS (Latin American and Caribbean Health Science Information database, from inception to 2 December 2024) We searched ClinicalTrials.gov ( clinicaltrials.gov/ ) and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) search portal ( apps.who.int/trialsearch/ ). For the COVID‐19 vaccines, we searched the following specific sources. Cochrane COVID‐19 Study Register for ongoing studies, not yet published studies, ( covid-19.cochrane.org ; inception to current; Appendix 2 ), which includes: PubMed, updated weekly; Embase.com , updated weekly; ClinicalTrials.com , updated daily; WHO ICTRP, updated weekly; and CENTRAL, updated monthly. WHO COVID‐19 global literature on coronavirus disease ( search.bvsalud.org/global-literature-on-novel-coronavirus-2019-ncov ) (from inception to June 2023, when manual updates to the database were discontinued). Searching other resources We handsearched the references of all the included studies and relevant review articles identified in the searches. If required, we contacted the authors for supplementary information. Furthermore, we searched for errata or retractions to our included studies published on MEDLINE, Embase, and Retraction Watch ( https://retractiondatabase.org/RetractionSearch.aspx? ) on 3 January 2025. Data collection and analysis Selection of studies For the RCT search, we applied the following two components of Cochrane's Screen4Me workflow to reduce the number of references retrieved and to assess the search results. Known assessment – a service that matches records in the search results to records that have already been screened in Cochrane Crowd and labeled as 'an RCT' or as 'not an RCT'. The RCT model ‐ a machine learning RCT classifier ( Wallace 2017 ), which is available in the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS‐Web). The RCT classifier assigns a probability of being a true RCT (from 0 to 100) to each citation. We assumed citations that were assigned a probability score below the cut point at a recall of 99% to be non‐RCTs. We manually dual‐screened those results that scored on or above the cut point. More information about Screen4Me, including evaluations, is available at the Screen4Me website on the Cochrane Information Specialist's portal (see Marshall 2018 ; McDonald 2017 ; Noel‐Storr 2018 ; Thomas 2017 ). Due to the relatively small number of references remaining, we did not use the third component, which would have consisted of consulting Cochrane Crowd, Cochrane's citizen science platform, where the Crowd helps to identify and describe health evidence. Two review authors (from AZ, NK, MB, and CH) independently screened the results of the search strategies for eligibility by reading the abstracts, using Rayyan software ( Ouzzani 2016 ). We obtained the full‐text publications of any abstracts that both review authors found eligible, and also of those that they disagreed about or rated as uncertain, for further discussion. Two review authors (from AZ, NK, MB, and CH) assessed the full‐text articles of selected studies. If the two review authors were unable to reach a consensus, we consulted a third review author (NS) to reach a final decision. We documented the study selection process in a flow chart, as recommended in the PRISMA statement, and showed the total number of retrieved references and the number of included and excluded studies ( Moher 2009 ). We listed studies that initially appeared to meet the inclusion criteria, but we later excluded, in the Characteristics of excluded studies table, along with the reasons for their exclusion. Data extraction and management Two review authors (from AZ, MB, YSP, and CH) extracted data independently and in duplicate, using a customized and piloted data extraction form developed in Microsoft Excel . We solved disagreements by discussion. If no agreement was obtained, we involved a third review author (NK). If multiple records of one study reported the same characteristics or outcome data, we choose the data with the longest follow‐up time. If required, we contacted the authors for supplementary information ( Boutron 2024 ). We collated multiple reports of each study so that the study, and not the report, was the unit of analysis. We extracted the following information, if reported. General information : author, title, source, publication date, publication type, country, language, ethics approval (yes/no), location of ethics committee, duplicate publications Study characteristics : trial design, setting and dates, source of participants, inclusion and exclusion criteria, length of follow‐up Participant characteristics : age, sex, ethnicity, number of participants recruited/allocated/evaluated, type of malignancy, stage of malignancy, details of anti‐cancer treatment (e.g. type of treatment, treatment status), additional diagnoses, previous known infection, recovery from infection, or previous vaccination (e.g. childhood) Intervention : type of vaccine and vaccination schedule, timing, duration of follow‐up For vaccines requiring multiple doses for full vaccination: time interval between shots, heterologous/homogeneous vaccination For booster vaccinations: time interval since full vaccination, type of booster vaccine Control intervention : placebo or no vaccine Outcomes as specified under Types of outcome measures Assessment of risk of bias in included studies For risk of bias assessments, we used tools tailored for RCTs or NSRIs, as appropriate. Two authors (from AZ, MB, and CH) independently assessed the risk of bias in included studies by outcome. When there were differences in judgment and inability to reach consensus, we consulted a third review author (NK) to reach a final decision. Randomised controlled trials For RCTs, we used the RoB 2 tool to analyse the risk of bias per study outcome listed for inclusion in the summary of findings tables ( Sterne 2019 ). Of interest in this review was the effect of the assignment to the intervention, that is, the intention‐to‐treat (ITT) effect. We assessed the following types of bias ( Higgins 2024c ). Bias arising from the randomisation process Bias due to deviations from the intended interventions Bias due to missing outcome data Bias in measurement of the outcome Bias in selection of the reported result For cluster‐randomised trials, we had planned to add a domain to assess bias arising from the timing of identification and recruitment of participants in relation to timing of randomisation ( Eldridge 2021 ; Higgins 2024b ). For cross‐over studies, we had planned to use the RoB 2 tool, because we only considered results from the first period before cross‐over ( Higgins 2024b ). To address these types of bias, we used the signalling questions recommended in RoB 2, and made a judgment using one of the following responses. Yes Probably yes No Probably no No information We used the algorithms proposed by RoB 2 to assign each domain one of the following levels of bias. Low risk of bias Some concerns High risk of bias Subsequently, we judged the overall risk of bias rating for each prespecified outcome in each study in accordance with the following recommendations within the RoB 2 tool. Low risk of bias: low risk of bias for all domains Some concerns: some concerns in at least one domain but no high risk of bias judgment for any domain High risk of bias: high risk of bias in at least one domain, or we judged the trial to have some concerns in multiple domains in a way that substantially lowered confidence in the results We used the RoB 2 Excel tool to implement RoB 2 (available from riskofbias.info ), and we stored and presented our detailed RoB 2 assessments as supplementary online material (available at Supplementary material RoB 2 ). Controlled non‐randomised studies of interventions For controlled NRSIs, we used the Risk of Bias in Non‐randomised Studies of Interventions (ROBINS‐I) tool ( Sterne 2016 ). The risk of bias assessment depended upon information on the design, conduct, and analysis of the study. We assessed the following domains of bias. Bias due to confounding Bias in selection of participants into the study Bias in classification of interventions Bias due to deviations from intended interventions Bias due to missing data Bias in measurement of outcomes Bias in selection of the reported result For every criterion, we made a judgment using one of five response options. Yes Probably yes Probably no No No information There were four levels for domain risk of bias judgments as follows. Low risk of bias Moderate risk of bias Serious risk of bias Critical risk of bias Subsequently, we derived an overall risk of bias rating for each prespecified outcome in each study, in accordance with the following recommendations ( Sterne 2016 ). Low risk of bias: low risk of bias for all domains Moderate risk of bias: low or moderate risk of bias for all domains Serious risk of bias: serious risk of bias in at least one domain, but not at critical risk of bias in any domain Critical risk of bias: critical risk of bias in at least one domain We used robvis, an online risk of bias visualisation tool for controlled NRSI, to create 'traffic light' plots of domain‐level judgments for each individual result ( McGuiness 2021 ). Our detailed ROBINS‐I assessments are available as an online supplement to the review at Supplementary material ROBINS-I . Measures of treatment effect For continuous outcomes, we planned to record the mean, standard deviation (SD), and total number of participants in both intervention and control groups. Where continuous outcomes used the same scale, we planned to use the mean difference (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). For continuous outcomes measured on different scales, we planned to use the standardised mean difference (SMD). However, data for continuous outcomes was not available. For dichotomous outcomes, we recorded the number of events and the total number of participants in both intervention and control groups. We reported the pooled risk ratio (RR) with a 95% CI ( Deeks 2024 ). For non‐RCTs, we preferentially extracted and used adjusted RRs with 95% CI. For cluster‐randomised trials, we planned to extract and report direct estimates of the effect measure (e.g. RR with a 95% CI) from an analysis that accounted for the clustered design. We planned to obtain statistical advice to ensure the analysis was appropriate. If appropriate analysis was not available, we planned to make every effort to approximate the analysis ( Higgins 2024b ). However, we did not include cluster‐RCTs. Unit of analysis issues The aim of this review was to summarise studies that analysed data at the level of the individual. For dichotomous outcomes (e.g. adverse events), we used participants as the unit of analysis, rather than events (e.g. the number of participants with adverse events rather than the number of events per participant ( Higgins 2024b )). If a study reported rate ratios, we analyzed the rate ratios on the basis of events rather than participants ( Higgins 2024d ). For cluster‐randomised studies, when study authors used an analysis that accounted for clustering, such as multilevel or generalized models, we planned to directly incorporate the effect estimate using inverse‐variance meta‐analysis. If the authors did not account for clustering, we planned to estimate the effective sample size or inflated standard error from the non‐accounted effect estimate, the number of clusters, and the intra‐class correlation coefficient for inclusion in meta‐analysis ( Higgins 2024b ). For cross‐over trials, we planned to only consider results from the first period before cross‐over. Studies with multiple treatment groups For studies with multiple treatment groups of the same intervention (i.e. dose), we evaluated whether study arms were sufficiently homogeneous to be combined. When it was not feasible to combine arms, we compared each arm with the common comparator separately. For pair‐wise meta‐analysis, we had planned to split the ‘shared’ group into two or more groups with smaller sample sizes, and include two or more (reasonably independent) comparisons. For this purpose, for dichotomous outcomes, both the number of events and the total number of participants would be divided; for continuous outcomes, the total number of participants would be divided by unchanged means and SDs ( Higgins 2024d ). However, this scenario did not occur. Dealing with missing data In the case of unclear or missing data (e.g. relevant participant characteristics), we contacted the corresponding authors of the studies. When we did not receive a response, or inclusion in the review and subsequent data extraction and analysis were not feasible, we categorized the study as 'awaiting classification'. When possible, we extracted effect estimates or data to calculate effect estimates for all allocated participants according to the intention‐to‐treat principle. If individuals allocated to treatment were missing from the analysis, we considered the possible effect of this on the analysis in our RoB assessment. Assessment of heterogeneity We planned to assess the heterogeneity of treatment effects between studies using a Chi 2 test, with a significance level of P < 0.1. We used the I 2 statistic to quantify possible heterogeneity (an I 2 statistic between 30% and 60% may signify moderate heterogeneity, between 50% and 90% may signify substantial heterogeneity, and over 75% may signify considerable heterogeneity ( Deeks 2024 )). Had heterogeneity been considerable in a meta‐analysis, we had planned to explore potential causes through sensitivity and subgroup analysis, and only present the meta‐analysis if the heterogeneity could be explained. If we had not been able to find a reason for heterogeneity, we would have commented on results from the individual studies and presented these in tables. However, this scenario did not occur. Assessment of reporting biases We searched in study registries to identify completed studies that had not been published elsewhere, in order to minimize or determine publication bias. We intended to explore potential publication bias by generating a funnel plot and statistically testing this, by conducting a linear regression test for meta‐analyses involving at least 10 trials ( Page 2024 ). We considered P < 0.1 as significant for this test. Data synthesis We conducted separate meta‐analyses for vaccines for different infectious diseases. We did not combine data from RCTs and controlled non‐randomised studies of interventions. If the clinical and methodological characteristics of individual studies were sufficiently homogeneous, we pooled the data in meta‐analysis according to the recommendations of the Cochrane Handbook, using Review Manager (RevMan) ( Deeks 2024 ; RevMan 2024 )). One review author (CH) entered the data into the software, and a second review author (AB) checked the data for accuracy. We used the random‐effects model for meta‐analysis, for both RCTs and controlled NRSIs, because we anticipated that true effects were related but not the same for all the included studies. For binary outcomes originating from RCTs, we estimated the between‐study variance using the Mantel‐Haenszel method. We used the inverse‐variance method for outcomes where hazard ratios (HR) were available. We had planned to use the inverse‐variance method for continuous outcomes and outcomes that included data from cluster‐RCTs. However, data for continuous outcomes or cluster‐RCTs were not available. Based on the guidance in Chapter 24 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions , we meta‐analysed controlled NRSI data when studies were considered sufficiently homogeneous, reported sufficient data, and were rated as low or moderate risk of bias, following the same approach as described for meta‐analysis of RCTs ( Reeves 2024 ). If we could not perform a meta‐analysis, we presented the results in forest plots without a combined effect estimate, according to vaccines for each infectious disease and subgroups (e.g. age, biological sex of participants, type of malignancy), and we provided a narrative commentary. Subgroup analysis and investigation of heterogeneity To explore heterogeneity, we planned to perform subgroup analysis for our critical outcome, incidence of the infection concerned, based on the following characteristics. Different types of vaccine for the same disease Alternative dosing regimens or schedules Age of participants (e.g. 18 to 75 years versus 75 years and above) Sex of participants (male versus female) Type of malignancy Stage of malignant disease (e.g. active versus in remission; treatment‐naïve versus first‐line treatment versus relapsed or refractory) Type of treatment (e.g. B‐cell‐depleting therapies, targeted or novel antineoplastic agents, chemotherapy) Treatment status (before therapy, during therapy, during maintenance therapy, after therapy) Vaccination schedule (duration between vaccinations; heterologous versus homologous (heterologous refers to the use of different vaccines for different doses, while homologous refers to the use of the same vaccine for all doses); time interval to booster shot) Due to differences in vaccine responses, we expected a higher incidence of infection in the following categories: elderly, males, B cell‐depleting therapies, during and before treatment, homologous vaccinations, and longer follow‐up periods. Moreover, different vaccine types and dosing regimens or schedules could contribute to heterogeneity. We planned to use the tests for interaction in RevMan to test for differences between subgroup results. Where only one study was available, we could not perform subgroup analysis. Sensitivity analysis We had planned sensitivity analysis for our critical outcome, incidence of the infection concerned, for the following criteria. Risk of bias assessment components: RCT with a low risk of bias or some concerns versus those with a high risk of bias; non‐randomised studies with a low risk of bias versus those with a moderate risk of bias; non‐randomised studies with a serious or critical risk of bias will not be included in any analysis Comparison of peer‐reviewed articles with non‐peer reviewed data sources (e.g. preprints, abstracts, data extracted from trial registries) We planned to use the tests for interaction to test for differences between our primary analysis and sensitivity analysis. Where only one study was available, we could not perform sensitivity analysis. Summary of findings and assessment of the certainty of the evidence Summary of findings tables We created separate summary of findings (SoF) tables for vaccines for each infectious disease compared to placebo or no vaccine ( Schünemann 2024 ). The order of the SoF tables was prioritised by clinical experts based on their relevance to decision‐makers. We presented the following outcomes in the SoF tables, prioritised by clinical experts, people with cancer, and their representatives. Incidence of the infection concerned (using methods as defined in the respective study) All‐cause mortality (at longest follow‐up available) Quality of life, if measured at a time point most commonly reported in studies, if the reported time points differ significantly, we will choose the longest follow‐up available Number of participants with any grade adverse events at longest follow‐up available Number of participants with serious adverse events at longest follow‐up available Number of participants with localised events at the injection site (e.g. tenderness or soreness, erythema, arm stiffness) Number of participants with systemic events (e.g. myalgia, fever, headache, fatigue, rash) at the longest follow‐up available If evidence from both RCTs and controlled NRSIs was available for a single outcome, we presented only the RCT data in the SoF tables. Assessment of the certainty of the evidence We used the GRADE approach to assess the certainty of the evidence for the outcomes listed in the previous section. The GRADE approach uses five domains (risk of bias, consistency of effect, imprecision, indirectness, and publication bias) to grade the certainty of the body of evidence for each outcome. Two authors (from AZ, NK and CH) independently assessed the certainty of each outcome. Disagreements were resolved by a third author (NK or NS). If we had serious or very serious concerns in any of the above domains, we downgraded our certainty of the evidence by one, two or three levels as follows. Study limitations: moderate (‐1) or serious (‐2) risk of bias; in addition, for non‐randomised studies (‐3) for critical risk of bias Inconsistency: serious (‐1) or very serious (‐2) inconsistency Indirectness: serious (‐1) or very serious (‐2) uncertainty about directness Imprecision: serious (‐1) or very serious (‐2) imprecise or sparse data Publication bias: serious (‐1) or very serious (‐2) probability of reporting bias The GRADE system uses the following criteria for assigning grades of evidence. High certainty: we are very confident that the true effect lies close to that of the estimate of the effect. Moderate certainty: we are moderately confident in the effect estimate; the true effect is likely to be close to the estimate of effect, but there is a possibility that it is substantially different. Low certainty: our confidence in the effect estimate is limited; the true effect may be substantially different from the estimate of the effect. Very low certainty: we have very little confidence in the effect estimate; the true effect is likely to be substantially different from the estimate of effect. We followed the current GRADE guidance for these assessments ( Schünemann 2024 ). In according with GRADE guidance 18, we started our initial rating for non‐randomised studies with high certainty (as for RCTs), as we used the ROBINS‐I tool to assess risk of bias ( Schünemann 2019 ). We used the overall risk of bias judgment to inform our decisions about downgrading for risk of bias. We phrased the findings and certainty of the evidence as suggested in the GRADE guidance on informative statements ( Santesso 2020 ). Results Description of studies Results of the search For RCTs, we searched all databases up to 2 December 2024 and screened the resulting records. We identified 72,317 records. After removing duplicates (n = 45,806), we removed another 11,552 records that were classified as unlikely to be RCTs by the RCT Classifier. We screened 14,959 records based on their titles and abstracts. We excluded 14,015 records that did not meet the prespecified inclusion criteria. Of the remaining 944 records, we included 25 records: five RCTs (21 records) on vaccines to prevent herpes zoster, influenza, or COVID‐19 for inclusion in this review; one ongoing RCT (one record) on vaccines to prevent influenza; three RCTs (three records) on vaccines to prevent pneumococcal disease and influenza awaiting classification as randomisation is unclear, recruitment status is unknown or has been reported as completed, but the results have not yet been published. We searched for prospective controlled NRSIs for vaccines against all infectious diseases (see Types of interventions ) except herpes zoster as we had identified RCTs for this disease. This included vaccines to prevent influenza and COVID‐19, as the RCTs we identified were published as correspondence or reported data on participants with solid tumours in a post hoc subgroup analysis. We searched all databases up to 2 December 2024 and screened the resulting records. In total, we identified 48,017 records. After removing duplicates (n = 28,677), we screened 19,340 records based on their titles and abstracts. We excluded 19,058 records that did not meet the prespecified criteria. Of the remaining 282 records, we included 22 records on controlled NRSIs: five controlled NRSIs (in 10 records) on vaccines to prevent influenza or COVID‐19 for inclusion in this review; one ongoing controlled NRSI (one record) on COVID‐19; 11 controlled NRSIs (in 11 records) on vaccines to prevent pneumococcal disease, influenza, or COVID‐19 are awaiting classification as recruitment status is unknown, the control group is unclear, no outcomes of interest were reported, results for participants with solid tumours are not reported separately, or follow‐up after full vaccination is unclear. The studies were selected according to the PRISMA guideline ( Moher 2009 ). The study selection process is illustrated in flow diagrams: Figure 1 for RCTs and Figure 2 for controlled NRSIs. The studies included 81,823 adults with solid tumours. One study was published as a correspondence article ( Goldmann 2015 ), and the remaining studies were published as full‐text publications ( Amdisen 2024 ; Gögenur 2021 ; INVIDIa‐2 ; Wijn 2018 ; Mullane 2013 ; Mullane 2019 ; Thomas 2022 ; Vink 2019 ; Zhao 2024 ). Three RCTs evaluated vaccines to prevent herpes zoster ( Mullane 2013 ; Mullane 2019 ; Vink 2019 ); five studies (one RCT and four controlled NRSIs) evaluated vaccines to prevent influenza ( Amdisen 2024 ; Gögenur 2021 ; INVIDIa‐2 ; Wijn 2018 ; Goldmann 2015 ); and two studies (one RCT and one controlled NRSI) investigated vaccines to prevent COVID‐19 ( Thomas 2022 ; Zhao 2024 ). We did not identify RCTs or controlled NRSIs of vaccines for the prevention of pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, or diphtheria in adults with solid tumours. All three RCTs were multicentric studies. Vink 2019 was conducted in Canada, the Czech Republic, France, the Republic of Korea, and the UK, while the other two RCTs did not report any details about the study sites ( Mullane 2013 ; Mullane 2019 ). The studies included 3054 participants with solid tumours recruited between November 2007 to April 2017. The mean age ranged between 55.8 to 64 years (range 35 to 83), and 64.6% of the participants were female. In two RCTs, participants were randomised to receive four doses of inactivated ( Mullane 2019 ) or heat‐treated ( Mullane 2013 ) varicella zoster vaccine, 30 days apart, compared to placebo. In Vink 2019 , participants were randomised to receive either two doses of an adjuvant recombinant zoster vaccine 30 to 60 days apart or placebo. One study reported data on the incidence of herpes zoster (mean 2.45 years after final dose) defined as confirmed herpes zoster (confirmed by skin lesion PCR, if available, or by adjudication of the clinical case description by the clinical adjudication committee) and all‐cause mortality up to 28 days after final dose ( Mullane 2019 ). All three RCTs reported data on safety outcomes, such as any adverse events and serious adverse events up to 30 days after final dose ( Mullane 2013 ; Mullane 2019 ; Vink 2019 ). Additional outcomes included antibody response ( Mullane 2013 ; Vink 2019 ), cell‐mediated immune response ( Mullane 2019 ; Vink 2019 ), and moderate‐to‐severe herpes zoster‐associated pain, herpes zoster complications, postherpetic neuralgia, and the number of participants with study medication withdrawn due to an adverse event ( Mullane 2019 ). The three RCTs were funded by the manufacturers of the vaccines ( Mullane 2013 ; Mullane 2019 ; Vink 2019 ). Studies of vaccines for the prevention of influenza Goldmann 2015 was a double‐blind RCT conducted in one centre in Germany. Four studies were prospective controlled NRSIs ( Amdisen 2024 ; Gögenur 2021 ; INVIDIa‐2 ; Wijn 2018 ). Three studies were open‐label and conducted in multiple centres in Italy ( INVIDIa‐2 ), Denmark ( Gögenur 2021 ), and the Netherlands ( Wijn 2018 ). Amdisen 2024 was a nationwide register‐based study conducted in Denmark. Altogether, the studies included data from 76,372 participants with solid tumours receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors (alone or in combination) ( INVIDIa‐2 ), participants with lung cancer receiving nivolumab ( Wijn 2018 ), participants with solid tumours scheduled for surgery ( Gögenur 2021 ), participants who were scheduled for surgery of neck or oesophageal cancer ( Goldmann 2015 ), and participants with an incident cancer diagnosis from 1 October 2002 to 1 October 2017 in the Danish Cancer Registry ( Amdisen 2024 ). In Amdisen 2024 , all participants received chemotherapy. Participants were recruited between November 2005 to January 2020 ( Gögenur 2021 ; INVIDIa‐2 ; Wijn 2018 ; Goldmann 2015 ). In Amdisen 2024 , the study period spanned from the introduction of the free‐of‐charge influenza vaccine for individuals with acquired immunodeficiency in the 2007/2008 season until the 2017/2018 season. The mean age ranged between 56.5 (SD 8.8) to 64.4 years (SD 7.8), and 6.1% to 55.3% of the participants were female ( INVIDIa‐2 ; Wijn 2018 ; Goldmann 2015 ). In Goldmann 2015 , participants were randomised to receive either two doses of an influenza vaccine (Mutagrip; Sanofi Pasteur) or placebo, administered on the day before surgery and the day of surgery. In the controlled NRSIs, participants received single doses of a trivalent seasonal influenza vaccine (influenza season 2015/2016 and 2016/2017) ( Wijn 2018 ), trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine ( Gögenur 2021 ), or trivalent adjuvant, trivalent non‐adjuvant, or quadrivalent non‐adjuvant influenza vaccine (influenza season 2019/2020) ( INVIDIa‐2 ) compared to no vaccine. In Gögenur 2021 , 26.2% of participants received the vaccine within 30 days post‐surgery, while 73.8% were vaccinated within 180 days of surgery. Amdisen 2024 gathered data on influenza vaccination dates from three Danish registries: the Danish National Health Service Register for free vaccinations administered by general practitioners, the Danish National Patient Registry for vaccinations during hospitalisation, and the Danish National Prescription Registry for vaccines redeemed at pharmacies. Notably, one individual could have been included in more than one influenza season. Two studies reported the incidence of influenza ( Amdisen 2024 ; INVIDIa‐2 ). In Amdisen 2024 , the outcome was defined as influenza requiring treatment based on an influenza diagnosis recorded in the Danish National Patient Registry or a prescription for oseltamivir documented in the Danish National Prescription Registry. In INVIDIa‐2 , the outcome was defined as a severe illness, characterised by sudden and rapid onset of one or more general symptoms, such as fever or low‐grade fever, malaise, and/or fatigue, headaches, myalgia, and at least one respiratory symptom such as cough, sore throat, or dyspnoea. Two studies reported all‐cause mortality 15 days post‐surgery and from 180 days to three years post‐surgery ( Gögenur 2021 ; Goldmann 2015 ), while Amdisen 2024 reported all‐cause mortality for up to five years after the first cancer diagnosis or until the end of the study period (31 March 2018), whichever came first. Two studies reported adverse events ( Wijn 2018 ; Goldmann 2015 ). Additional outcomes include duration of hospital and ICU stay, mHLA‐DR expression of monocytes, postoperative incidence of infections ( Goldmann 2015 ); time to influenza‐like illness, Influenza‐free survival, vaccine cover rate, incidence of bacterial complications, infection recrudescence, clinically diagnosed complications/ superinfections during the influenza episode, hospital admissions, and need for intravenous therapy for influenza‐like illness, duration of influenza symptoms, influenza‐like illness fatality rate, usage rate for the quick test/nasal/pharyngeal swab or viral serology in people with influenza‐like illness, disease control rate, objective response rate, time to treatment failure, progression‐free survival, overall survival, immune‐related toxicity ( INVIDIa‐2 ); immune‐related adverse events and serious adverse events, discontinuation owing to immune‐related serious adverse events, progression, or clinical deterioration ( Wijn 2018 ); pneumonia, myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure, venous thromboembolism ( Amdisen 2024 ). INVIDIa‐2 was funded by the manufacturer of the vaccine, whereas Goldmann 2015 received funding from inner university grants. Amdisen 2024 received public funding from the Danish Cancer Research Foundation and the Danish Cancer Society. Two studies did not disclose their funding sources ( Gögenur 2021 ; Wijn 2018 ). Studies of vaccines for the prevention of COVID‐19 Thomas 2022 was a triple‐blind RCT conducted in multiple centres across the USA, Argentina, Brazil, Germany, South Africa, and Turkey. Zhao 2024 was a prospective controlled multicentric NRSI conducted in China. Altogether, the studies included data from 2397 participants with solid tumours. In Thomas 2022 , the total population originally was 46,429 healthy participants aged over 12 years. However, participants with pre‐existing stable neoplasia, including solid tumours and haematological malignancies, were also eligible to participate in the study. For this population, Thomas 2022 analysed the data in a post‐hoc subgroup analysis. Zhao 2024 included participants with hepatocellular carcinoma. Participants were recruited between July 2020 and January 2021 ( Thomas 2022 ) or between January 2022 and October 2022 ( Zhao 2024 ). Based on the recruitment periods, we assume that participants may have been exposed to the SARS‐CoV‐2 variants alpha, beta, and gamma ( Thomas 2022 ) or omicron ( Zhao 2024 ). The mean age ranged between 59.2 (SD 11) and 62 years (SD 11.8). In Thomas 2022 , most participants (62.7% to 63.9%) were female, whereas in Zhao 2024 , only 17.6% to 20.6% were female. In Thomas 2022 , participants were randomised to receive either two doses of BNT162b2 or placebo. In Zhao 2024 , participants received at least one dose of various vaccines, including CoronaVac, BBIBP‐CorV, Ad5‐nCoV, BNT162b2, ZF2001 (an adjuvant protein subunit vaccine, not authorised by the EMA or authorised in at least 10 countries worldwide) or no vaccine. Each of these vaccines typically consists of two doses. Notably, 44.9% of the participants completed the full two‐dose regimen, while 48.6% received a booster vaccination. Some of the participants (6.5%) had only one dose and were therefore not fully vaccinated. Thomas 2022 reported the incidence of COVID‐19, defined as a positive reverse transcription chain reaction (RT‐PCR) or nucleic acid amplification technology (NAAT) test in participants without previous SARS‐CoV‐2 infection, and in participants with and without previous SARS‐CoV‐2 infection from seven days up to six months after the second dose. Additionally, the study reported adverse events and serious adverse events in a mixed population of individuals with solid tumours and haematological malignancies who had a past or ongoing malignancy. Zhao 2024 reported on the incidence of COVID‐19, defined as the rate of SARS‐CoV‐2 infections over a median follow‐up period of 16.3 months (interquartile range (IQR) 14.2 to 19.3). However, it was not specified whether SARS‐CoV‐2 infections were confirmed by testing. The study also provided data on all‐cause mortality. Additional outcomes included vaccine efficacy ( Thomas 2022 ), overall survival, infection‐free survival, severe or very severe SARS‐CoV‐2 infection, and vaccine‐related adverse events ( Zhao 2024 ). Thomas 2022 received funding from the manufacturer of the vaccine, while Zhao 2024 was supported by public funding. Ongoing studies We identified two ongoing studies, which the study registrations classified as ‘recruiting’ ( NCT05774171 ) or 'recruitment completed' ( ACTRN12622000706774 ) (see Characteristics of ongoing studies ). NCT05774171 is a prospective cohort study evaluating COVID‐19 vaccines compared to no vaccine in participants with past or current tumours, regardless of tumour type. The target sample size is 700 participants, and the planned completion date is recorded as December 2023. ACTRN12622000706774 is an open‐label RCT investigating an influenza vaccine compared to no vaccine in participants undergoing major abdominal cancer surgery. The target sample size is 54 participants and the planned completion date is recorded as March 2024. Up to 28 days after the final dose, 124 of 1379 participants in the vaccine group and 107 of 1365 participants in the comparator group had died. Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster probably make little or no difference in all‐cause mortality up to 28 days after final dose compared to placebo (RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.50; I² = 0%; 2 RCTs, 2744 participants; moderate‐certainty evidence; Analysis 1.2 ). We downgraded the certainty of the evidence to one level for serious imprecision due to a wide confidence interval.
